Cornell Suspends Fraternity Parties Amid Sexual Assault Allegations

October 14, 2026
Share
Facebook
Twitter
Pinterest
Linkedin
Email
Print
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 1:20
    Instaread

    Cornell University will suspend parties and social events at fraternity houses until the end of the academic year following mounting backlash over allegations of sexual assault on campus in 2024. The decision follows a lawsuit filed in September by a former student, Jane Doe, who alleges that seven men sexually assaulted her during a fraternity party. None of the men named in the lawsuit has been criminally charged. University President Michael Kotlikoff said the suspension would allow officials to review fraternity life and determine how it can operate safely.

    The university has faced protests from students, criticism from faculty and alumni, and pressure from donors over its handling of the case. The investigation has been reopened, and New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as an independent special prosecutor. Cornell will also work with New York State Police to investigate incidents and accelerate recommendations from a task force on sexual violence. The university plans to hire additional staff to support survivors.

    The controversy has intensified concerns about campus safety. A 2025 university survey found that 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing non-consensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since enrolling at Cornell. Kotlikoff acknowledged that many women on campus continue to question their safety and said the university must recognize its shortcomings and take meaningful action.
